items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 22.19 Optical isomerism in drug molecules

items.label: text
items.text: An important application of optical isomerism is in the synthesis of pharmaceutical drugs. You might have heard of the thalidomide tragedy. Back in the 1960s in Germany, the molecule B shown in Figure 22.19 was found to have anti-nausea effects and was therefore used to treat morning sickness in pregnant woman. Unfortunately, molecule B was being manufactured together with its optical isomer A and little was known about the molecule A until many children born in that era were found to have deformed limbs. These days, many drug companies devote a great deal of money to separating optical isomers of new drugs just in case they have side effects.

items.label: section_header
items.text: ETHENEAND PROPENE

items.label: text
items.text: Ethene, CH2=CH2, doesn't have any isomers. Propene, CH3CH=CH2, doesn't have a structural isomer that is still an alkene.

items.label: section_header
items.text: EXTENSIONWORK

items.label: text
items.text: There is a structural isomer of C₃H6 that doesn't have a carbon-carbon double bond. It has three carbon atoms joined in a ring. It is called cyclopropane, which indicates 'a ring of three carbons with only single bonds between them'.

items.label: text
items.text: There are three structural isomers with the molecular formula CH8and containing a carbon-carbon double bond.

items.text: Figure 22.20 Structural isomers with the molecular formula of C4H8.

items.label: text
items.text: Notice the way that you can vary the position of the double bond as well as branching the chain.

items.label: section_header
items.text: A QUICK INTRODUCTORY LOOK AT THE ALCOHOLS

items.label: text
items.text: Alcohols are a homologous series of compounds which all contain an -OH functional group attached to a hydrocarbon chain. This is coded for in the name by the ending'-ol'.
